I guess I hadn't thought of patenting as such an invention in and of itself (probably because I was thinking about things that wouldn't/couldn't be patented), but that does make a lot of sense. Documentation has always been one of the most important components of engineering.

There's a lot of this in military tech and tactics. My favourite example is pike or spear formations. I don't know exactly how various civilizations influenced each other in this, but prior to the proliferation of firearms the eventual culmination of arms races was generally a variation of organized formations of men with long pointy sticks. The classical Greeks and Macedonians had their phalanges, the renaissance Swiss had pike squares, and the Japanese, contrary to popular belief, relied heavily on yari formations at the height of their warring period. Even after firearms became the arms of choice infantry people kept on using pike formations for quite a while

It tickles me that with all the intricate weapons and fighting styles of the medieval world many civilizations eventually defaulted to forming up into rectangles holding sharp poles.
Ha, good point. Would you happen to know if swords and archery and cavalry started like this, or just spread? I know horses had to have come from one place, but what about other animals?

No one can really tell for sure how the essential staples spread, so a lot of this early history is based on guesswork. I suspect that cavalry spread from a single point, probably in Eurasia or the middle east. Although the Americas did indeed have wild horses (and camels), wild horses are actually too small to be ridden, and a considerable amount of coexistence and breeding is required before you can field mounted troops. That's why the first cavalry was made up of charioteers; either their horses were to weak to mount, or they just hadn't conceived of the idea yet. Archery as well seems like an abstract enough concept (the stick bends and the string throws tiny spears?) that it wasn't developed in parallel by everyone, although it's not ruled out.

Swords, however, were quite possibly developed by separate civilizations because they follow naturally from knives; as long as you've got the metalworking skill, you might as well make a longer knife to gain the advantage, right? Even the indigenous South Americans, who didn't have the metalworking skills, had sword-like Macuahuitl
